Neonatal bonnet macaques emerge weighing approximately 300 grams [Wwb = approximately 300 grams], a relatively modest birth mass that places them within the expected range for cercopithecine primates of similar adult body size. This initial investment by the mother is followed by an extended period of intense maternal care. In captive colonies maintained at a consistent thermoneutral temperature of 37.3 °C [T = 37.3 °C], gestation has been recorded as lasting 161 days [tg = 161 days], a duration typical for macaque species. The relatively short gestational period compared to the total developmental trajectory underscores the altricial nature of neonatal macaques, which are entirely dependent on their mothers for thermoregulation, transport, and nutrition during the first weeks of life.

The suckling period in this species extends for a considerable duration before the juvenile transitions to nutritional independence. Under standard captive conditions at 37.3 °C [T = 37.3 °C], weaning is typically completed at 304 days since birth [tx = 304 days since birth], marking the end of lactation-dependent offspring status. This prolonged nursing phase allows for substantial somatic growth and the gradual acquisition of social skills vital for life in complex multi-male, multi-female groups. After weaning, the juvenile enters a lengthy period of growth and social learning before the onset of reproductive capability.

Sexual maturation in female bonnet macaques occurs after an extended period of post-weaning growth. Under the same thermal regime of 37.3 °C [T = 37.3 °C] used in most primate research facilities, females typically reach puberty at 1275 days since birth [tp = 1275 days since birth]. This onset of gonadal activity is associated with significant size dimorphism that becomes apparent as individuals approach adulthood. Males, in contrast, undergo a markedly different developmental timeline, with puberty occurring much later at 1795 days since birth [tp = 1795 days since birth] at a temperature of 37.3 °C [T = 37.3 °C]. This delayed maturation in males is thought to reflect the competitive pressures of the social system, where larger body size confers reproductive advantages.

Adult body mass in the bonnet macaque exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism, a common pattern among macaques. Females reach an ultimate wet weight of approximately 5500 grams [Wwi = approximately 5500 grams], while males achieve a far greater adult body mass of 11600 grams [Wwi = 11600 grams]. This nearly two-fold difference in mass represents one of the more extreme examples of size dimorphism within the genus Macaca and is linked to male-male competition for access to estrous females. The energetic demands of maintaining such a large body size influence male reproductive strategies and ranging behavior across the species' distribution in southern India.

Longevity records from captive populations of Macaca radiata indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 35 years [am = approximately 35 years] when animals are housed under optimal conditions at 37.3 °C [T = 37.3 °C]. This extended lifespan is consistent with a slow life-history strategy that prioritizes somatic maintenance over rapid reproduction. The maximum reproductive rate observed in well-fed captive females is approximately one offspring per year [Ri = approximately one offspring per year], with each pregnancy yielding a single infant [N_R_i = each pregnancy yielding a single infant], a reproductive output that reflects the high maternal investment in each offspring. This combination of extended lifespan, prolonged development, and low annual fecundity places the bonnet macaque firmly among the slow end of the primate life-history continuum.
